problem: The trap says a student who writes speedup S = n when p = n² is wrong, and blames fan-in and broadcast. But at p = n² each processor owns one whole output cell and does n multiply-adds, so the ideal speedup against one processor is n² = p, not n. The chapter's own model gives S = n³/(n + log n²), close to n². As written the trap teaches a value wrong by a factor of n, and the reason given (fan-in per dot product) does not apply when one processor owns a whole cell.
fix: Writing speedup S = n² (= p) when p = n², as if the dot products cost only their multiplications. The model S = n³/(n³/p + log p) gives S ≈ n³/(n + log n²), a little below n², because the reduction and vector-broadcast overhead sit in the denominator.

problem: Both the question and the answer are wrong. The question asks why the speedup is not n at p = n², and the answer says S is below n. With p = n² the ideal speedup is p = n², and the chapter's formula gives S ≈ n², which is far above n. The answer contradicts the formula in Section 3.
fix: Q4: Why is the speedup not exactly n² (= p) when p = n²? Answer: each of the n² processors finishes its own length-n dot product, so the arithmetic alone gives speedup n²; the model denominator adds the broadcast and reduction overhead log p, so S stays a little below n² and flattens once that overhead is comparable to n³/p.

problem: The schedule described (each round, broadcast a[i][k] along row i and b[k][j] down column j) is not Cannon's algorithm. Cannon's algorithm skews the initial alignment of the blocks and then uses nearest-neighbour circular shifts of A left and B up; it uses no row or column broadcast. Calling the broadcast schedule Cannon's will confuse students who meet the real algorithm later.
fix: Drop the Cannon sentence here, or say: Cannon's algorithm is a different mesh schedule, in which blocks are skewed at the start and then, in each of n rounds, every cell does one multiply-add and passes its A value one step left and its B value one step up.

problem: 'The time is O(n³/p) only when the cells divide evenly' is too strong. With p ≤ n², the busiest processor holds ⌈n²/p⌉ cells, so its time is ⌈n²/p⌉·n, which is still O(n³/p + n) = O(n³/p). Uneven division changes the constant, not the order.
fix: The time is Θ(n³/p); uneven division adds at most one extra cell, that is n extra steps, which does not change the order when p ≤ n². Load balance matters for the constant factor.

problem: The figure is drawn with 0-based indices (index_from 0) but the row is labelled 'B col 1' while showing B's first column [5,7] (index 0), and it is matched to c₁₁, which uses 1-based subscripts. A student can read 'col 1' as the second column and expect [6,8].
fix: Label the row 'B column 1 (first column)' and keep the c₁₁ subscript notation, or label the whole figure with indices 0 and use c[0][0].

problem: The setup gives four processors, one per cell of C, but step 9 says x is broadcast 'to both processors' without saying which two. With n = 2 the matrix-vector product needs two processors (one per row of A), not four.
fix: Say: y has n = 2 entries, so two processors, one per row of A, each need every entry of x; x is broadcast to those two before the row dot products start.
